study.title: John 2 - Signs of the glory of Jesus and the purification of the temple
study.overview: John 2 presents two decisive acts at the beginning of Jesus" public ministry: the sign in Cana, in which the water destined for purification is transformed into excellent wine, and the purification of the temple, in which Jesus rejects the religious trade and declares that the zeal for the house of God consumes it. The chapter also shows different answers before Jesus: the disciples believe, many are impressed by the signs, but Jesus does not surrender to their superficial trust because he knows the human interior.

outline.title: The Marriage in Cana and the First Sign
outline.explanation: Jesus meets the need for the feast, transforms water into wine and manifests its glory. The miracle is not only provision, but a sign that points to who he is and to the joy associated with his presence.

outline.title: The trip to Capernaum and the purification of the temple
outline.explanation: After the sign in Cana, Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for the Passover and casts out of the temple those who turned it into a place of trade. His gesture shows prophetic authority and zeal for the holiness of the Father's house.

outline.title: The sign requested and the reference to the temple of the body
outline.explanation: The Jews demand credentials for Jesus" attitude, and he answers with a word about destroying and rebuilding the temple in three days. John clarifies that Jesus spoke of the temple of his body, which the disciples only fully understood after the resurrection.

outline.title: Faith based on signs and the knowledge of Jesus about the human being
outline.explanation: Many begin to believe when he sees the signs, but Jesus does not entrust himself to them, because he knows everyone and knows what is inside each person. The closing of the chapter contrasts true faith with superficial adherence.

study.context: The chapter mentions a marriage in Cana of Galilee and the Passover in Jerusalem, two occasions linked to the religious life of the Jewish people. Notes highlight that the marriage could last several days and that the stone pots were used in purification ceremonies. They also indicate that the activity in the temple was related to the need to offer approved sacrifices at the Passover feast, which had generated a trade within the sacred enclosure. The biblical text, however, details nothing more than that, and it is advisable to avoid explanations beyond what the chapter itself and the notes inform.
study.theology: John 2 teaches that Jesus inaugurates something new without despising the previous revelation. In the sign of Cana, the water of purification is replaced by wine, suggesting superiority and fullness in relation to the ancient rites. In the cleansing of the temple, Jesus acts as the one who has authority over the Father's house and on the worship of God. The reference to the temple of his body anticipates that his death and resurrection will be the true center of worship. The chapter also corrects a faith merely based on visible evidence: signs may arouse interest, but Jesus knows the heart and is not deceived by superficial adements. Thus, the glory of Christ is revealed in concrete acts, but requires a response of deep faith, not only passing admiration.

scholarViews.insight: The notes understand the purification of the temple as a prophetic act by which Jesus demanded that the house of God be returned to his own purposes: worship, prayer, instruction, and sacrifice.
The notes note that although many believed because of the signs, Jesus did not trust them because he knew them too well to surrender to confidence in superficial faith.
The notes claim that Jesus knew everything and knew each person, because he knows the human interior and distinguishes the sincere from the hypocrites.

questions: What difference is there between admiring the signs of Jesus and believing in him in fact, as the disciples did?
In which areas of Christian life can I be treating what is holy as something utilitarian or commercial, as occurred in the temple?
What changes in my decisions when I remember that Jesus knows my interior and not just my religious appearance?
study.practice: This passage calls the reader to obey Jesus promptly, as the servants in Cana did, and to allow him to purify what is mixed with unfit interests in worship and life. It also invites a deeper faith: instead of relying only on emotions or signs, seeking a mature trust in the person of Christ, whose glory is manifested in his work, his death and his resurrection. In practice, this means examining one's own heart, abandoning religiosity of facade and cultivating reverence, sincerity and concrete obedience.
study.uncertainty: There are important limits in the material provided: it is not possible to determine with certainty the identity of the wedding feast, the exact relationship between Jesus" hour and the rest of the gospel, nor the chronology of the episode of temple purification beyond what the notes allow. Nor should it be appropriate to affirm as a historical fact details that appear only as a hypothesis in one of the commentators, such as the possibility of being John's marriage. The readings of commentators on the order of events and some details of the text should be treated as interpretations, not as mandatory conclusions of the chapter.
